Chapter 7: The Value of Impermanence.
Have you ever felt that quiet little fear—the one that whispers, "What if this good thing doesn't last?" We all know it. We try to hold on to happy moments, wishing we could freeze time. There’s this almost universal ache when we notice youth slipping away, or when love changes, or the thrill of a big success starts to fade. It's natural to crave something permanent. But, as you and I both know, life just doesn’t work that way. Everything keeps shifting.
Picture this: you're with close friends, having that perfect evening. Laughter fills the room, your worries are miles away, and for that little while, life just feels... right. But then, the night winds down. Suddenly, there's this bittersweet feeling—because you know you can't bottle up that moment, no matter how much you want to.
That longing for things to stay exactly the same? It’s so deeply human. But here’s something to pay attention to: in every tradition, there’s a lesson that impermanence is the only real constant. Everything changes—our relationships, our careers, our health... even who we are inside. And honestly, the more we try to resist that, the more we end up struggling.
Think about someone who’s just retired. They look back on years of work—the habits, the sense of purpose, the daily chats with coworkers—and suddenly, all of that is just... gone. At first, there's this heavy feeling of loss. Maybe even a temptation to keep reaching back for what’s already passed. But then, over time, a new view starts to open up. Retirement brings a kind of freedom: time for hobbies, deeper family bonds, space to finally reflect. Sure, the loss is real. But so is the chance for something new to blossom.
Buddhist philosophy talks about impermanence a lot—not as a reason to despair, but as a way to truly appreciate what we have while we have it. When you really understand that nothing lasts forever, every moment starts to shine a little brighter. The beauty of a sunset, the warmth of a hug, even your favorite meal—they all become more precious because they’re fleeting.
Most of us don’t realize just how much energy we use fighting change. But when we finally loosen that grip—when we stop resisting—a kind of peace quietly moves in. The fear of losing what we love shifts, and we start to feel grateful for what’s here, right now.
Or take a young couple, facing the end of their relationship. There’s grief, there’s regret, and the urge to hold on feels overwhelming. But eventually, acceptance finds its way in. The memories are still there. But so is the possibility of something new. The pain of impermanence? It’s real. But so is the gift: a chance to begin again.
Maybe, in the end, impermanence isn’t our enemy at all. It’s a wise teacher. It nudges us to cherish what we have, to let go when the time comes, and to trust the unfolding story of our lives.
